From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

709 Crackdown on Human Rights Lawyers

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Native name | 中国709维权律师大抓捕事件 |
| English name | 709 Crackdown |
| Date | 9 July 2015 |
| Location | * [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing"), China |
| Target | Human rights lawyers, civil rights defenders, activists |
| Organized by | [General secretaryship of Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_secretaryship_of_Xi_Jinping "General secretaryship of Xi Jinping"), [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party"), [Ministry of Public Security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Public_Security_(China) "Ministry of Public Security (China)") |
| Outcome | Repression of Chinese civil society and arrest of hundreds of human rights lawyers, [disbarment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disbarment "Disbarment") |
| Arrests | 300+ |
| Charges | [Subversion of state power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inciting_subversion_of_state_power "Inciting subversion of state power"), [picking quarrels and provoking trouble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picking_quarrels_and_provoking_trouble "Picking quarrels and provoking trouble") |

The **709 Crackdown** ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_language "Chinese language"): 中国709维权律师大抓捕事件; [pinyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinyin "Pinyin"): *Zhōngguó 709 wéiquán lǜshī dàzhuābǔ shìjiàn*; lit. 'China 709 mass arrest of civil rights lawyers incident' or 709案 '709 Case' for short) was a nationwide crackdown on [Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") lawyers and [human rights activists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_activist "Human rights activist") during the summer of 2015. It is known as the "709 crackdown" as it started on 9 July 2015.[[1]](#cite_note-bbc-2017-05-22-1)

Yaqiu Wang of [Human Rights Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Rights_Watch "Human Rights Watch") commented that "the 709 crackdown dealt a terrible blow to [China's rights-defense movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weiquan_movement "Weiquan movement"), which significantly contracted as rights lawyers were jailed, [disbarred](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disbarred "Disbarred") or placed under surveillance".[[2]](#cite_note-latimes-2018-12-26-2)

More than 300 people were detained as part of the 2015 crackdown.[[3]](#cite_note-bbc-2017-12-26-3) Some of the notable people affected by the crackdown are listed below.

* [Li Heping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Heping "Li Heping"), former human rights lawyer who was abducted in 2015. He was then given a suspended jail term in April 2017,[[4]](#cite_note-4) and released in May 2017.[[5]](#cite_note-5)
* [Wang Quanzhang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Quanzhang "Wang Quanzhang"), arrested in August 2015, stood trial from December 2018 to January 2019, sentenced to 4.5 years imprisonment for subversion of state power,[[6]](#cite_note-6) and released from prison on 4 April 2020. Moved by authorities to his former residence in [Jinan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jinan "Jinan") for two-week [COVID-19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19") isolation period; his wife believes the government used the epidemic as an excuse to keep him under house arrest.[[7]](#cite_note-bbc-2020-04-08-7)
* [Wang Yu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Yu_(lawyer) "Wang Yu (lawyer)"), lawyer charged with [inciting subversion of state power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inciting_subversion_of_state_power "Inciting subversion of state power"), but released on bail in 2016.
* [Wu Gan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wu_Gan "Wu Gan"), human rights activist known as the "Super Vulgar Butcher", who was sentenced to eight years in December 2017.
* [Xiang Li](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xiang_Li_(activist) "Xiang Li (activist)"), activist forbidden from leaving China during the crackdown, but who was smuggled out of China to [Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand "Thailand") in January 2018.

On 17 June 2020, according to a [Deutsche Welle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutsche_Welle "Deutsche Welle") report, [Yu Wensheng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yu_Wensheng "Yu Wensheng"), who had defended Wang Quanzhang and publicly called for the removal of [General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Secretary_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party") [Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping") as well as for reforms in the legal and political systems, was sentenced to four years in prison and deprived of political rights for three years.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

A decade later, in 2025, some of the lawyers affected have begun to speak out publicly about the continued deterioration of legal freedoms in China.

Ren Quanniu, a disbarred human rights lawyer who initially avoided repercussions during the 709 crackdown, has described a sharp decline in the legal environment for rights defenders, particularly since the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_mainland_China "COVID-19 pandemic in mainland China"). He likened the current state of the [rule of law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_of_law "Rule of law") in China to the [Cultural Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Revolution "Cultural Revolution"), a period during which judicial institutions were largely dismantled. Ren, who had represented citizen journalist [Zhang Zhan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhang_Zhan "Zhang Zhan") after her arrest for reporting on the early COVID-19 outbreak in [Wuhan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wuhan "Wuhan"), was formally disbarred in 2021. He and other former rights lawyers contend that the legal profession in China has been fundamentally transformed, leaving little to no space for human rights advocacy under current conditions.[[9]](#cite_note-:0-9)

[Jiang Tianyong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiang_Tianyong "Jiang Tianyong"), a former lawyer who was imprisoned for "inciting subversion", emphasized that the rights defense movement was not intended to challenge the state but to work within China's existing legal framework. He noted that while the movement achieved limited success, its efforts made it more difficult for authorities to target vulnerable groups.[[9]](#cite_note-:0-9)

According to human rights organizations and researchers, the crackdown has become more systematic and less visible in recent years, involving increased restrictions on legal professionals and greater control by the [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP) over law firms. Lawyers handling politically sensitive cases have had their licenses revoked, and many are subjected to ongoing surveillance and travel bans.[[9]](#cite_note-:0-9)

**Falun Gong**,[[a]](#cite_note-2) also called **Falun Dafa**,[[b]](#cite_note-3) is a [new religious movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_religious_movement "New religious movement") founded by [Li Hongzhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Hongzhi "Li Hongzhi") in [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") in the early 1990s. Falun Gong has its global headquarters in [Dragon Springs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dragon_Springs "Dragon Springs"), a 173-hectare (427-acre) compound in [Deerpark, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deerpark,_New_York "Deerpark, New York"), United States, near the residence of Li.[[2]](#cite_note-JUNKER-2019-33-101-4)[[3]](#cite_note-VAN-DER-MADE-2019-5)[[4]](#cite_note-COLLINS-2019-6)[[5]](#cite_note-7)

Falun Gong emerged from the [qigong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qigong "Qigong") movement in China in 1992, combining meditation, qigong exercises, and moral teachings rooted in Buddhist and Taoist traditions.[[6]](#cite_note-Ownby_(2003)-8)[[7]](#cite_note-9) While initially supported by some government agencies in China,[[8]](#cite_note-OW-10)[[9]](#cite_note-BayFang-11) Falun Gong's rapid growth and independence from state control led several top officials in China to perceive it as a threat, resulting in periodic acts of harassment in the late 1990s.[[10]](#cite_note-FC-12)[[11]](#cite_note-O8-13)[[12]](#cite_note-14) On 25 April 1999, over 10,000 Falun Gong practitioners gathered peacefully outside the central government compound in Beijing, seeking official recognition of the right to practice their faith without interference.[[13]](#cite_note-15)[[14]](#cite_note-CC-16)

In July 1999, the [government of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_China "Government of China") implemented a ban on Falun Gong, categorizing it as an "illegal organization". Mass arrests, widespread torture and abuses followed.[[15]](#cite_note-FG-17)[[16]](#cite_note-18) In 2008, U.S. government reports cited estimates that as much as half of China's labor camp population was made up of Falun Gong practitioners.[[17]](#cite_note-KM-19)[[18]](#cite_note-AR-20) In 2009, human rights groups estimated that at least 2,000 Falun Gong practitioners had died from persecution by that time.[[19]](#cite_note-nytimes.com-21) Falun Gong practitioners also face systematic societal discrimination in employment, education, housing, and business opportunities.[[20]](#cite_note-GC-22)[[21]](#cite_note-Slaughter-23)[[22]](#cite_note-24) Prior to its 1999 ban on Falun Gong, the Chinese government estimated there were 70 million adherents.[[23]](#cite_note-Faison-25)[[24]](#cite_note-Schoff-26)[[25]](#cite_note-US-DEPT-STATE-2022-27) In 2009, Falun Gong sources estimated that tens of millions continue to practice privately.[[20]](#cite_note-GC-22)[[25]](#cite_note-US-DEPT-STATE-2022-27)[[26]](#cite_note-28) A 2017 Freedom House report estimated there were between 7 and 20 million practitioners in China at the time.[[27]](#cite_note-29)[[28]](#cite_note-30)[[25]](#cite_note-US-DEPT-STATE-2022-27)

Led by Li Hongzhi, Falun Gong practitioners operate a variety of organizations in the United States and elsewhere, including the dance troupe [Shen Yun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shen_Yun "Shen Yun").[[29]](#cite_note-Carolyn_Maloney-31)[[30]](#cite_note-The_Observer-32) The Falun Gong also operates the Epoch Media Group, which is known for its subsidiaries, [New Tang Dynasty Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Tang_Dynasty_Television "New Tang Dynasty Television") and *[The Epoch Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Epoch_Times "The Epoch Times")* newspaper. The latter has been broadly noted as a politically [far-right](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far-right_politics "Far-right politics")[[31]](#cite_note-33) media entity, and it has received significant attention in the United States for promoting conspiracy theories, such as [QAnon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QAnon "QAnon") and [anti-vaccine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-vaccine "Anti-vaccine") misinformation, and producing advertisements for [U.S. President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._President "U.S. President") [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"). It has also drawn attention in Europe for promoting far-right politicians, primarily in [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France") and [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany").[[32]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHettena2019-34)[[33]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPerroneLoucaides2022-35) The media have noted Falun Gong's opposition to the [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP), its negative views on [homosexuality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homosexuality "Homosexuality") and [feminism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feminism "Feminism"), and its [objections to evolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Objections_to_evolution "Objections to evolution").[[34]](#cite_note-36)

## Beliefs and practices

Falun Gong is based around the teachings of its founder and leader, Li Hongzhi. According to *NBC News*, "To his followers, Li is a God-like figure who can levitate, walk through walls and see into the future. His ultra-conservative and controversial teachings include a rejection of modern science, art and medicine, and a denunciation of homosexuality, feminism and general worldliness."[[35]](#cite_note-NBC-ZARDROZNY-2023-37)

A series of [protests against COVID-19 lockdowns](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protests_against_responses_to_the_COVID-19_pandemic "Protests against responses to the COVID-19 pandemic") began in [mainland China](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_China "Mainland China") in November 2022.[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[4]](#cite_note-:0-4)[[7]](#cite_note-:1-7)[[8]](#cite_note-:2-8)[[9]](#cite_note-:3-9) Colloquially referred to as the **White Paper Protests** ([Chinese](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Chinese_characters "Simplified Chinese characters"): 白纸抗议; [pinyin](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinyin "Pinyin"): *Bái zhǐ kàngyì*) or the **A4 Revolution** (Chinese: 白纸革命; pinyin: *Bái zhǐ gémìng*),[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11) the [demonstrations](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_demonstration "Political demonstration") started in response to [measures](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_government_response_to_COVID-19 "Chinese government response to COVID-19") taken by the [Chinese government](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_government "Chinese government") to prevent the spread of [COVID-19 in the country](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_mainland_China "COVID-19 pandemic in mainland China"), including implementing a [zero-COVID](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero-COVID "Zero-COVID") policy. Discontent had grown since the beginning of the pandemic towards the policy, which confined many people to their homes for prolonged periods of time without work and left some unable to purchase or receive daily necessities.[[12]](#cite_note-:5-12)[[13]](#cite_note-13)

The demonstrations had been preceded by the [Beijing Sitong Bridge protest](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing_Sitong_Bridge_protest "Beijing Sitong Bridge protest") on 13 October, wherein pro-democracy banners were displayed by an unnamed individual and later seized by local authorities. The incident was subsequently censored by state media and led to a widespread crackdown behind the [Great Firewall](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Firewall "Great Firewall").[[14]](#cite_note-cnn_anti-xi-14) Further small-scale protests inspired by the Sitong Bridge incident ensued in early November, before widespread civil unrest erupted following a [24 November building fire](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Ürümqi_fire "2022 Ürümqi fire") in [Ürümqi](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ürümqi "Ürümqi") that killed ten people,[[a]](#cite_note-RFA44-16) three months into a [lockdown](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_lockdown_in_China "COVID-19 lockdown in China") in Xinjiang.[[16]](#cite_note-17) Protesters across the nation demanded the end of the government's zero-COVID policy and lockdowns.[[7]](#cite_note-:1-7)

The subjects in protest evolved throughout the course of the unrest, ranging from discontent with the leadership of the [Chinese Communist Party](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP) and its [general secretary](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Secretary_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party") [Xi Jinping](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping"),[[7]](#cite_note-:1-7)[[17]](#cite_note-CNN1127-18) to inhumane working conditions brought on by the lockdowns, and [human rights abuses](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Uyghurs_in_China "Persecution of Uyghurs in China") against ethnic [Uyghurs](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyghurs "Uyghurs") in Xinjiang.[[18]](#cite_note-19) The police had largely allowed such rallies to proceed, although officers had reportedly arrested several protesters in Shanghai.[[19]](#cite_note-BBC_News-20) There had also been reports of protesters being beaten and showered with [pepper spray](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pepper_spray "Pepper spray") before detainment.[[19]](#cite_note-BBC_News-20)[[20]](#cite_note-crowd_angered-21)[[21]](#cite_note-:6-22)[[22]](#cite_note-Lau_Politico-23) By early December, China pivoted away from many of its previous COVID restrictions by reducing testing, reducing lockdowns, and allowing people with mild infections to quarantine at home, effectively abandoning the zero-COVID policy.[[23]](#cite_note-CFR_policy-24)

These lockdowns began with the [lockdown](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_lockdown_in_China "COVID-19 lockdown in China") of [Wuhan](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wuhan "Wuhan") in January 2020, and soon spread to other cities and municipalities, including Shanghai and [Xinjiang](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang "Xinjiang"). As these lockdowns became more widespread, they became lengthier and increasingly disruptive, precipitating increasing concern and dissent. The **Beijing Sitong Bridge protest** was a protest that took place on October 13, 2022, in [Haidian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haidian,_Beijing "Haidian, Beijing"), [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing"), China.

The protest happened three days before the opening of the [20th National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_National_Congress_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "20th National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party") (CCP). On the morning of October 13, 2022, a protester demonstrated against [CCP general secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Secretary_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party") [Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping")'s [cult of personality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping's_cult_of_personality "Xi Jinping's cult of personality"), [dictatorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_secretaryship_of_Xi_Jinping "General secretaryship of Xi Jinping"), [human rights violations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_in_China "Human rights in China"), strengthening of [censorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Censorship_in_China "Censorship in China"), seeking of [leadership for life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_for_life "President for life") and implementation of the [zero-COVID](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero-COVID "Zero-COVID") policy by hanging banners and burning tires on [Sitong Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sitong_Bridge?action=edit&redlink=1 "Sitong Bridge (page does not exist)") [[zh](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%9B%9B%E9%80%9A%E6%A1%A5 "zh:四通桥")] ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Chinese_characters "Simplified Chinese characters"): 四通桥; [pinyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinyin "Pinyin"): *Sìtōng Qiáo*) in Haidian, Beijing.

The protester, [Peng Lifa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peng_Lifa "Peng Lifa") (彭立发; pinyin: Péng Lìfā; b. 1974),[[1]](#cite_note-1) has been dubbed Bridge Man or Banner Man in reference to [Tank Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tank_Man "Tank Man").

Protests took place frequently in China in the 2000s, with 180,000 protests taking place in 2010 according to [Tsinghua University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsinghua_University "Tsinghua University") sociology professor Sun Liping.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

This protest against Xi Jinping and his policies was rare, as it came just days before the start of the CCP National Congress, a period during which the authorities imposed extremely tight control over protests and dissent. It was widely expected that Xi's rule for an unprecedented third term would be cemented at the Congress.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-:2-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-:3-7)[[8]](#cite_note-8)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/%E5%9B%9B%E9%80%9A%E6%A9%8B%E6%8A%97%E8%AD%B0%E8%80%85%E8%A2%AB%E5%B8%B6%E4%B8%8A%E8%AD%A6%E8%BB%8A.png/250px-%E5%9B%9B%E9%80%9A%E6%A9%8B%E6%8A%97%E8%AD%B0%E8%80%85%E8%A2%AB%E5%B8%B6%E4%B8%8A%E8%AD%A6%E8%BB%8A.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%E5%9B%9B%E9%80%9A%E6%A9%8B%E6%8A%97%E8%AD%B0%E8%80%85%E8%A2%AB%E5%B8%B6%E4%B8%8A%E8%AD%A6%E8%BB%8A.png)

The protest was held on October 13, 2022, on [Sitong Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4th_Ring_Road#North_4th_Ring_Road "4th Ring Road") by a lone protester. The protester, having disguised himself as a construction worker by wearing an orange vest and a yellow helmet, placed two banners on the bridge and set fire to tires to produce attention-drawing smoke. He then repeatedly chanted through a loudspeaker, "Go on strike at school and work, remove dictator and national traitor Xi Jinping! We want to eat, we want freedom, we want to vote!"[[11]](#cite_note-bbc-11) He was soon arrested by security forces.[[12]](#cite_note-12)[[13]](#cite_note-:0-13) [Radio Free Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_Free_Asia "Radio Free Asia") reported in October 2023 that he was still alive, whereabouts "unclear," with his family under close surveillance.[[14]](#cite_note-14)

Photos of the event spread rapidly on [online social media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_networking_service "Social networking service").[[15]](#cite_note-15)[[16]](#cite_note-16)

Peng Lifa also published a 23-page detailed [promotional document](#External_links) on [ResearchGate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ResearchGate "ResearchGate"), calling on the public to begin boycotting classes and work, as well as honking car horns and other activities, starting on October 16 (the opening day of the 20th National Congress, a Sunday).[[17]](#cite_note-yvette-17)[[18]](#cite_note-william-18)

Though [The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times") published an article on December 7, 2022, naming him "[Peng Lifa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peng_Lifa "Peng Lifa")", the protester's identity has not been confirmed. However, some believe him to be an academic physicist and have flooded a Twitter account assumed to be linked to the protester with messages of admiration.[[11]](#cite_note-bbc-11) [The Wall Street Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wall_Street_Journal "The Wall Street Journal") and [Radio Free Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_Free_Asia "Radio Free Asia") reported that some activists believed the protester to be Peng Lifa, also known as Peng Zaizhou, a 48-year-old physics enthusiast.[[19]](#cite_note-19)[[20]](#cite_note-20)

Protest banner themes included [Xi Jinping's cult of personality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping's_cult_of_personality "Xi Jinping's cult of personality"), dictatorship and totalitarian rule, infringement of [human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_in_China "Human rights in China"), strengthening of [censorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Censorship_in_China "Censorship in China"), Xi Jinping's [reelection despite failure to observe term limits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abolition_of_the_lifetime_tenure_system_for_leading_cadres "Abolition of the lifetime tenure system for leading cadres"), the [Cultural Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Revolution "Cultural Revolution"), the implementation of the "[zero-COVID](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero-COVID "Zero-COVID")" policy, and [overwork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overwork "Overwork").[[21]](#cite_note-:5-21)[[22]](#cite_note-22)[[13]](#cite_note-:0-13)[[23]](#cite_note-23)[[24]](#cite_note-24)

**Peng Lifa** ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Chinese_characters "Simplified Chinese characters"): 彭立发; [pinyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinyin "Pinyin"): *Péng Lìfā*; born January 7, 1974[[1]](#cite_note-DW_2024-1)) is a Chinese [democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy_movements_of_China "Democracy movements of China") activist who initiated the [Beijing Sitong Bridge protest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing_Sitong_Bridge_protest "Beijing Sitong Bridge protest") in October 2022 before the [20th National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_National_Congress_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "20th National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party"). He was named one of the [100 most influential people in the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_100 "Time 100") by *[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")* magazine in 2023.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)

## Career and activism

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Peng_Lifa&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Career and activism")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/70/%E5%9B%9B%E9%80%9A%E6%A9%8B%E6%8A%97%E8%AD%B0%E8%80%85%E8%A2%AB%E5%B8%B6%E4%B8%8A%E8%AD%A6%E8%BB%8A.png/250px-%E5%9B%9B%E9%80%9A%E6%A9%8B%E6%8A%97%E8%AD%B0%E8%80%85%E8%A2%AB%E5%B8%B6%E4%B8%8A%E8%AD%A6%E8%BB%8A.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%E5%9B%9B%E9%80%9A%E6%A9%8B%E6%8A%97%E8%AD%B0%E8%80%85%E8%A2%AB%E5%B8%B6%E4%B8%8A%E8%AD%A6%E8%BB%8A.png)

Peng (dressed in orange) was brought into a police vehicle, on Sitong Bridge.

Peng worked for an acrylic products firm called Beijing Melon Network Technology Co., Ltd.[[5]](#cite_note-:1-5) He wrote articles on [electromagnetism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetism "Electromagnetism").[[5]](#cite_note-:1-5)

On October 13, 2022, Peng initiated the [Beijing Sitong Bridge protest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing_Sitong_Bridge_protest "Beijing Sitong Bridge protest") by posting a banner on the [Sitong Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sitong_Bridge?action=edit&redlink=1 "Sitong Bridge (page does not exist)") [[zh](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%9B%9B%E9%80%9A%E6%A1%A5 "zh:四通桥")].[[6]](#cite_note-:0-6) Peng draped protest banners from Beijing's Sitong Bridge. They unfurled to reveal exhortations against China's [zero-COVID policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero-COVID_policy "Zero-COVID policy"), calling it a violation of freedom of expression and demanding real elections and political reform.

Peng further challenged [General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Secretary_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party") [Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping") on October 13, 2022, by shouting through a loudspeaker, "We want to eat. We want freedom. We want votes!." He is suspected to have been detained by the police.[[5]](#cite_note-:1-5) His slogans spread across the country with comparisons being made between Peng and the [Tank Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tank_Man "Tank Man").[[6]](#cite_note-:0-6) His act was described by [BBC News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_News "BBC News") as "one of the most significant acts of Chinese protest seen under [Xi's rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_secretaryship_of_Xi_Jinping "General secretaryship of Xi Jinping")."[[7]](#cite_note-bbc-7)

Though the *[New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")* published an article on December 7, 2022, naming him "Peng Lifa," the protester's identity has not been confirmed.[[7]](#cite_note-bbc-7) However, some believe him to be an academic physicist and have flooded a Twitter account assumed to be linked to the protester with messages of admiration.[[7]](#cite_note-bbc-7) *[The Wall Street Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wall_Street_Journal "The Wall Street Journal")* and [Radio Free Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_Free_Asia "Radio Free Asia") reported that some activists believed the protester to be Peng Lifa, also known as Peng Zaizhou, a 48-year-old physics enthusiast.[[8]](#cite_note-8)[[9]](#cite_note-9)

In April 2023, Peng was named to the [*Time* 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_100 "Time 100") list of the most influential people in the world for his pro-democracy activism.[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11)

As of October 2023, according to sources familiar with the case cited by [VOA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voice_of_America "Voice of America"), Peng Lifa remained in detention at a location described as unknown.[[2]](#cite_note-VOA_2023-2)

Peng Lifa's family continues to face significant government scrutiny and control. His close family members are under constant surveillance and have not been provided with any legal documents related to his case. Despite efforts, his relatives and friends have been unable to hire a lawyer to provide him with legal assistance.[[2]](#cite_note-VOA_2023-2)

Peng Lifa's wife and daughters are under strict government surveillance, with their every move accompanied by government personnel. Their daily commutes to work and school are arranged by the authorities, and their personal cell phones have been confiscated — ostensibly for "protection" — and replaced with government-issued phones. Peng's siblings have been summoned to the local police station for questioning. His father-in-law, previously a small business owner, has been reassigned by the [Public Security Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_security_bureau_(China) "Public security bureau (China)") to work and live in a small factory, where he remains under surveillance. His mother-in-law is also believed to be under surveillance. In addition, his two sisters-in-law, the husband of one of them, and his brother-in-law have been questioned at their workplaces.[[2]](#cite_note-VOA_2023-2)

Peng was born in 1974 in [Heilongjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heilongjiang "Heilongjiang").[[6]](#cite_note-:0-6)[[5]](#cite_note-:1-5) As of October 2023, his wife and two daughters, both of whom have been described as minors, all reside in [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing"). His brothers and sisters are farmers in [Tailai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tailai_County "Tailai County"), Heilongjiang Province, and his parents have both died due to illness.[[2]](#cite_note-VOA_2023-2)

The **Beijing Sitong Bridge protest** was a protest that took place on October 13, 2022, in [Haidian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haidian,_Beijing "Haidian, Beijing"), [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing"), China.

The protest happened three days before the opening of the [20th National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/20th_National_Congress_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "20th National Congress of the Chinese Communist Party") (CCP). On the morning of October 13, 2022, a protester demonstrated against [CCP general secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Secretary_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party") [Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping")'s [cult of personality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping's_cult_of_personality "Xi Jinping's cult of personality"), [dictatorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_secretaryship_of_Xi_Jinping "General secretaryship of Xi Jinping"), [human rights violations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_in_China "Human rights in China"), strengthening of [censorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Censorship_in_China "Censorship in China"), seeking of [leadership for life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_for_life "President for life") and implementation of the [zero-COVID](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero-COVID "Zero-COVID") policy by hanging banners and burning tires on [Sitong Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sitong_Bridge?action=edit&redlink=1 "Sitong Bridge (page does not exist)") [[zh](https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%9B%9B%E9%80%9A%E6%A1%A5 "zh:四通桥")] ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Chinese_characters "Simplified Chinese characters"): 四通桥; [pinyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinyin "Pinyin"): *Sìtōng Qiáo*) in Haidian, Beijing.

The protester, [Peng Lifa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peng_Lifa "Peng Lifa") (彭立发; pinyin: Péng Lìfā; b. 1974),[[1]](#cite_note-1) has been dubbed Bridge Man or Banner Man in reference to [Tank Man](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tank_Man "Tank Man").

Protests took place frequently in China in the 2000s, with 180,000 protests taking place in 2010 according to [Tsinghua University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsinghua_University "Tsinghua University") sociology professor Sun Liping.[[2]](#cite_note-2)

This protest against Xi Jinping and his policies was rare, as it came just days before the start of the CCP National Congress, a period during which the authorities imposed extremely tight control over protests and dissent. It was widely expected that Xi's rule for an unprecedented third term would be cemented at the Congress.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-:2-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-:3-7)[[8]](#cite_note-8)

The protest was held on October 13, 2022, on [Sitong Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4th_Ring_Road#North_4th_Ring_Road "4th Ring Road") by a lone protester. The protester, having disguised himself as a construction worker by wearing an orange vest and a yellow helmet, placed two banners on the bridge and set fire to tires to produce attention-drawing smoke. He then repeatedly chanted through a loudspeaker, "Go on strike at school and work, remove dictator and national traitor Xi Jinping! We want to eat, we want freedom, we want to vote!"[[11]](#cite_note-bbc-11) He was soon arrested by security forces.[[12]](#cite_note-12)[[13]](#cite_note-:0-13) [Radio Free Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_Free_Asia "Radio Free Asia") reported in October 2023 that he was still alive, whereabouts "unclear," with his family under close surveillance.[[14]](#cite_note-14)

Photos of the event spread rapidly on [online social media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_networking_service "Social networking service").[[15]](#cite_note-15)[[16]](#cite_note-16)

Peng Lifa also published a 23-page detailed [promotional document](#External_links) on [ResearchGate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ResearchGate "ResearchGate"), calling on the public to begin boycotting classes and work, as well as honking car horns and other activities, starting on October 16 (the opening day of the 20th National Congress, a Sunday).[[17]](#cite_note-yvette-17)[[18]](#cite_note-william-18)

Though [The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times") published an article on December 7, 2022, naming him "[Peng Lifa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peng_Lifa "Peng Lifa")", the protester's identity has not been confirmed. However, some believe him to be an academic physicist and have flooded a Twitter account assumed to be linked to the protester with messages of admiration.[[11]](#cite_note-bbc-11) [The Wall Street Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wall_Street_Journal "The Wall Street Journal") and [Radio Free Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_Free_Asia "Radio Free Asia") reported that some activists believed the protester to be Peng Lifa, also known as Peng Zaizhou, a 48-year-old physics enthusiast.[[19]](#cite_note-19)[[20]](#cite_note-20)

Protest banner themes included [Xi Jinping's cult of personality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping's_cult_of_personality "Xi Jinping's cult of personality"), dictatorship and totalitarian rule, infringement of [human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_in_China "Human rights in China"), strengthening of [censorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Censorship_in_China "Censorship in China"), Xi Jinping's [reelection despite failure to observe term limits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abolition_of_the_lifetime_tenure_system_for_leading_cadres "Abolition of the lifetime tenure system for leading cadres"), the [Cultural Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Revolution "Cultural Revolution"), the implementation of the "[zero-COVID](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zero-COVID "Zero-COVID")" policy, and [overwork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overwork "Overwork").[[21]](#cite_note-:5-21)[[22]](#cite_note-22)[[13]](#cite_note-:0-13)[[23]](#cite_note-23)[[24]](#cite_note-24)

Contents of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_in_China:
[Human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights "Human rights") in the [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_China "People's Republic of China") (PRC) are severely curtailed. [Freedom of speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_speech_in_China "Freedom of speech in China"), [freedom of the press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_the_press "Freedom of the press"), [freedom of religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_religion_in_China "Freedom of religion in China"), [freedom of assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_assembly "Freedom of assembly") and [workers' rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labor_rights "Labor rights") are restricted by the [government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_China "Government of China"). The [Chinese political system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_China "Politics of China") is [authoritarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Authoritarianism "Authoritarianism"), with no freely elected national leaders, and repression of political opposition, as well as a lack of [an independent judiciary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judicial_independence "Judicial independence"), [rule of law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_of_law "Rule of law"), and [due process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Due_process "Due process").[[1]](#cite_note-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2) Human rights abuses by the Chinese government are prevalent, with extensive [censorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Censorship_in_China "Censorship in China"),[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4) [mass surveillance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_surveillance_in_China "Mass surveillance in China"),[[5]](#cite_note-5) and repression of [ethnic minorities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnic_minorities_in_China "Ethnic minorities in China") and religious groups, including [Christians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity_in_China "Christianity in China"),[[a]](#cite_note-12) [Muslims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam_in_China_(1912%E2%80%93present) "Islam in China (1912–present)"), [Tibetan Buddhists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibetan_Buddhism "Tibetan Buddhism"), [Uyghurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyghurs "Uyghurs"),[[12]](#cite_note-13)[[13]](#cite_note-14) and groups the government deems as "cults" such as [Falun Gong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falun_Gong "Falun Gong").

The [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") and government's stated view of human rights emphasizes [economic development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_development "Economic development"), material well-being, and national [sovereignty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereignty "Sovereignty").[[14]](#cite_note-McGregor-15) They have often challenged notions of individual [civil and political rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_and_political_rights "Civil and political rights") in [international human rights law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_human_rights_law "International human rights law") as being [universal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_value "Universal value").[[15]](#cite_note-uc-16)[[16]](#cite_note-ds-17)

Academics, international [non-governmental organizations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-governmental_organization "Non-governmental organization") (NGOs) including [Human Rights in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Rights_in_China_(organization) "Human Rights in China (organization)") and [Amnesty International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amnesty_International "Amnesty International"), human rights treaty bodies and the [United Nations Human Rights Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Human_Rights_Council "United Nations Human Rights Council")'s [Universal Periodic Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Periodic_Review "Universal Periodic Review"),[[17]](#cite_note-18) as well as citizens, lawyers, and [dissidents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dissident "Dissident") inside the country, have documented how the authorities in [mainland China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_China "Mainland China") regularly sanction or organize abuses.[[18]](#cite_note-19)[[19]](#cite_note-20)[[20]](#cite_note-21) [Human rights groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_human_rights_organizations "China human rights organizations") have also raised concerns about the prevalent use of [capital punishment in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_punishment_in_China "Capital punishment in China"), the [one-child policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One-child_policy "One-child policy") (prior to abolishing it in 2015), and human rights in [Tibet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibet "Tibet"). In a human rights report that assesses social, economic, and political freedoms, China received the lowest ranking globally for safety from state actions and the right to assemble.[[21]](#cite_note-22)[[22]](#cite_note-amnesty.org-23)

Some survey data has indicated that citizens of the PRC prioritize the right to survival over political rights and the [World Values Survey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Values_Survey "World Values Survey") finds that 72% are satisfied with the state of human rights in their country.

Some Chinese activist groups are trying to improve human rights. [Chinese human rights attorneys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weiquan_movement "Weiquan movement") who take on cases related to these issues, however, often face harassment, disbarment, and arrest by the Chinese state.[[23]](#cite_note-HRW_Thin_Ice-24)[[24]](#cite_note-amnesty13-25)[[25]](#cite_note-26) [Democracy movements in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy_movements_of_China "Democracy movements of China") have been repressed, most notably in the [1989 Tiananmen Square massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1989_Tiananmen_Square_protests_and_massacre "1989 Tiananmen Square protests and massacre").[[26]](#cite_note-27)

Since the [legal reforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legal_history_of_China#1978-1981 "Legal history of China") of the late 1970s and 1980s, the CCP has officially moved to embrace the language of the [rule of law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_of_law "Rule of law"), and it has also attempted to establish a modern [court system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Court_system_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China "Court system of the People's Republic of China"). During this process, it has enacted thousands of new laws and regulations, and it has begun to train more [legal professionals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legal_profession "Legal profession").[[23]](#cite_note-HRW_Thin_Ice-24) The concept of 'rule of law' has been emphasized in the [constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_China "Constitution of China"), and the ruling party has embarked on campaigns to promote the idea that citizens have protection under the law. At the same time, however, a fundamental contradiction exists in the constitution itself, in which the CCP insists that its authority supersedes that of the law.[[27]](#cite_note-fordham-28) Thus, the constitution enshrines the rule of law and simultaneously stresses the principle that the "[leadership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generations_of_Chinese_leadership "Generations of Chinese leadership") of the Communist Party" holds primacy over the law and the legal system.[[28]](#cite_note-29)

The judiciary is not [independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judicial_independence "Judicial independence") of the CCP, and judges face political pressure; in many instances, private party committees dictate the outcome of cases.[[29]](#cite_note-30) In 2007, law and the judiciary were further subordinated to the interests of the CCP under the doctrine of the [Three Supremes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Supremes "Three Supremes").[[30]](#cite_note-31) In 2013, [Document Number Nine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Document_Number_Nine "Document Number Nine") detailed the CCP's antipathy toward the rule of law. This has produced a system often described as "rule *by* law" (alluding to the CCP's power), rather than rule *of* law.[[31]](#cite_note-nytimes-32) Moreover, the legal system lacks protections for [civil rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_law_(Common_law) "Civil law (Common law)"), and often fails to uphold due process.[[32]](#cite_note-33) This is opposed to a system of [checks and balances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checks_and_balances "Checks and balances") or [separation of powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separation_of_powers "Separation of powers").[[33]](#cite_note-34) Scholars have noted that these characteristics of the legal system in China often undermine due process in practice, particularly in politically sensitive criminal cases handled by defense lawyers, as analyzed in *[Criminal Defense in China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Criminal_Defense_in_China "Criminal Defense in China")*.[[34]](#cite_note-Cambridge_University_Press-35)

Foreign experts estimate that in 2000, there were between 1.5 million and 4 million people in prison in mainland China. The PRC does not allow outsiders to inspect its penal system.[[35]](#cite_note-Becker-36)

Rights in China resemble the European construct of [positive law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positive_law "Positive law"), informed by the legacy of the [Napoleonic Code](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleonic_Code "Napoleonic Code"), in which rights are created and granted by the state.[[36]](#cite_note-37): 60

Contents of https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Falun_Gong:
[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/Speaker_at_Washington_DC._STOP_the_Persecution_of_Falun_Gong.jpg/500px-Speaker_at_Washington_DC._STOP_the_Persecution_of_Falun_Gong.jpg)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Speaker_at_Washington_DC._STOP_the_Persecution_of_Falun_Gong.jpg)

Then-member of the [United States House of Representatives](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives"), [Ileana Ros-Lehtinen](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ileana_Ros-Lehtinen "Ileana Ros-Lehtinen"), who co-sponsored a congressional resolution condemning organ harvesting from Falun Gong adherents, speaks at a rally in Washington, D.C.



The **persecution of Falun Gong** is the campaign initiated in 1999 by the [Chinese Communist Party](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP) to eliminate the [new religious movement](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_religious_movement "New religious movement") [Falun Gong](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falun_Gong "Falun Gong") in [China](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"), maintaining a doctrine of [state atheism](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_atheism "State atheism").[[1]](#cite_note-1) It is characterized by a multifaceted propaganda campaign, a program of enforced ideological conversion and re-education and reportedly a variety of extralegal coercive measures such as arbitrary arrests, [forced labor](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forced_labor "Forced labor") and physical [torture](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torture "Torture"), sometimes resulting in [death](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death "Death").[[2]](#cite_note-Amnesty1-2)

Falun Gong was founded by its leader [Li Hongzhi](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Hongzhi "Li Hongzhi"), who introduced it to the public in May 1992 in [Changchun](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Changchun "Changchun"), [Jilin](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jilin "Jilin"). Li Hongzhi currently lives near [Dragon Springs](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dragon_Springs "Dragon Springs") in [Deerpark, New York](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deerpark,_New_York "Deerpark, New York"), where Falun Gong's global headquarters are.[[3]](#cite_note-NBC-ZARDROZNY-2023-3)[[4]](#cite_note-JUNKER-2020-B-4) Falun Gong combines meditation, [qigong](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qigong "Qigong") exercises, and moral teachings rooted in Buddhist and Taoist traditions.[[5]](#cite_note-Ownby_(2003)-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6) Following a period of rapid growth in the 1990s, the CCP launched a campaign to "eradicate" Falun Gong on 20 July 1999.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESpiegel2002-7)

The Chinese government had alleged that Falun Gong was an "evil cult" or "heretical sect" and had used that official rationale to justify to ban and eliminate the movement.[[8]](#cite_note-8)[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10) An extra-constitutional body called the [6-10 Office](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/6-10_Office "6-10 Office") was created to lead the persecution of Falun Gong.[[11]](#cite_note-CECC2008-11) The authorities mobilized the state media apparatus, judiciary, police, army, the education system, families and workplaces against the group.[[12]](#cite_note-wildgrass-12) The campaign was driven by large-scale propaganda through television, newspaper, radio and the Internet.[[13]](#cite_note-Leung-13) There are reports of systematic torture,[[14]](#cite_note-heretical-14)[[15]](#cite_note-breaking-15) illegal imprisonment, forced labor, [organ harvesting](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organ_harvesting_from_Falun_Gong_practitioners_in_China "Organ harvesting from Falun Gong practitioners in China")[[16]](#cite_note-orgharv-16) and abusive psychiatric measures, with the apparent aim of forcing practitioners to recant their belief in Falun Gong.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESpiegel2002-7)

Reports from the United States Congressional-Executive Commission on China and State Department include estimates that hundreds of thousands and perhaps millions of Falun Gong practitioners have been detained in "[re-education through labor](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Re-education_through_labor "Re-education through labor")" camps, prisons and other detention facilities for refusing to renounce the spiritual practice.[[11]](#cite_note-CECC2008-11)[[17]](#cite_note-Departmentof-17) Former prisoners have reported that Falun Gong practitioners consistently received "the longest sentences and worst treatment" in labor camps, and in some facilities Falun Gong practitioners formed the substantial majority of detainees.[[18]](#cite_note-HumanRights-18)[[19]](#cite_note-19) As of 2009, at least 2,000 Falun Gong practitioners had been reportedly tortured to death in the persecution campaign.[[20]](#cite_note-20) Some international observers and judicial authorities have described the campaign against Falun Gong as a [genocide](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genocide "Genocide").[[21]](#cite_note-21)[[22]](#cite_note-22) In 2009, courts in Spain and Argentina indicted senior Chinese officials for genocide and crimes against humanity for their role in orchestrating the suppression of Falun Gong.[[23]](#cite_note-reutersflg-23)[[24]](#cite_note-24)[[25]](#cite_note-25)

In 2006, allegations emerged that [many Falun Gong practitioners had been killed to supply China's organ transplant industry](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organ_harvesting_from_Falun_Gong_practitioners_in_China "Organ harvesting from Falun Gong practitioners in China").[[16]](#cite_note-orgharv-16)[[26]](#cite_note-CGOH-26) An initial [investigation](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilgour-Matas_report "Kilgour-Matas report") found that "the source of 41,500 transplants for the six-year period 2000 to 2005 is unexplained" and concluded that "there has been and continues today to be large scale organ seizures from unwilling Falun Gong practitioners".[[16]](#cite_note-orgharv-16) [Ethan Gutmann](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethan_Gutmann "Ethan Gutmann") estimates 65,000 Falun Gong practitioners were killed for their organs from 2000 to 2008.[[27]](#cite_note-Jay-27)[[28]](#cite_note-HMH-28) Following additional analysis, the researchers significantly raised the estimates on the number of Falun Gong practitioners who may have been targeted for organ harvesting.[[29]](#cite_note-independent.co.uk-29) In 2008, United Nations Special Rapporteurs reiterated their requests for "the Chinese government to fully explain the allegation of taking vital organs from Falun Gong practitioners and the source of organs for the sudden increase in organ transplants that has been going on in China since the year 2000".[[30]](#cite_note-MW-30)

## Background

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3c/Origins-GuangzhouPractice.jpg/330px-Origins-GuangzhouPractice.jpg)](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Origins-GuangzhouPractice.jpg)

Morning Falun Dafa exercises in [Guangzhou](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guangzhou "Guangzhou"). The banner reads "Falun Dafa Free-Teaching Exercise Site". Falun Gong's popularity worried senior officials of the [CCP](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CCP "CCP").[[31]](#cite_note-freedom_house-31)[[32]](#cite_note-Palmer-32)

Falun Gong, also known as Falun Dafa, is a new religious movement that combines meditation, [qigong](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qigong "Qigong") energy exercises, and moral guidance rooted in Buddhist and Taoist traditions.[[33]](#cite_note-33)[[34]](#cite_note-34)[[35]](#cite_note-35)[[36]](#cite_note-36) Falun Gong is based around the teachings of its founder and leader: China-born Li Hongzhi. According to *NBC News*, to his followers, Li is "a God-like figure who can levitate, walk through walls and see into the future. His ultra-conservative and controversial teachings include a rejection of modern science, art and medicine, and a denunciation of homosexuality, feminism and general worldliness."[[3]](#cite_note-NBC-ZARDROZNY-2023-3) Hongzhi instructs his followers to not talk about "Falun Gong's inner teachings" when talking to outsiders, contradictory to his teachings about "Truthfulness".[[37]](#cite_note-Lewis_2017-37)

The practice of Falun Gong was first taught publicly by Li in Northeast China in the spring of 1992, towards the end of China's "[qigong boom](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qigong_boom "Qigong boom")".[[38]](#cite_note-Ownby-38)[[32]](#cite_note-Palmer-32) Falun Gong initially enjoyed considerable official support during the early years of its development. It was promoted by the state-run Qigong Association and other government agencies. By the mid-1990s, however, Chinese authorities sought to rein in the influence of qigong practices and enacted more stringent requirements on the country's various qigong denominations.[[38]](#cite_note-Ownby-38) In 1995 authorities mandated that all qigong groups establish Communist Party branches. The government also sought to formalize ties with Falun Gong and exercise greater control over the practice. Falun Gong resisted co-optation, and instead filed to withdraw altogether from the state-run qigong association.[[32]](#cite_note-Palmer-32)

Following this severance of ties to the state, the group came under increasing criticism and surveillance from the country's security apparatus and [propaganda department of the Chinese Communist Party](//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propaganda_Department_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "Propaganda Department of the Chinese Communist Party"). Falun Gong books were banned from further publication in July 1996, and official news outlets began criticizing the group as a form of "feudal superstition", whose "theistic" orientation was at odds with the official ideology and national agenda.[[38]](#cite_note-Ownby-38)

Tensions continued to escalate through the late 1990s. # Lens 3B.2 — Xi Jinping (China), 2023

**Question:** Did the ruler prevent, punish, or tolerate abuse by police, military, intelligence services, prisons, militias, party enforcers, informal loyalists, or tolerated vigilantes?

**One-sentence answer for 2023:** The 2023 record is **strongly negative** — Xi tolerated, expanded, and directed the very security apparatus whose abuse was the substantive concern of the lens. The 2023 PLARF leadership purge (July–October 2023), the anti-corruption–framed removal of the defense minister, the multi-year political sentences for human-rights lawyers and Uyghur intellectuals, the Hong Kong NSL prosecutions, the Counterespionage Law / Religious Activity Venues Measures / Patriotic Education Law expansion, the surveillance-tech tracking (TikTok LGBT), the cross-border abductions (Yang Zewei, Lu Siwei), the Sitong-Bridge protester Peng Lifa's continued secret detention into October 2023 and beyond, the harassment of the Wenzhou retiree-protest participants, the "Basil" Peng Lifa's family surveillance, the 20 million + 2 million internet-commentator apparatus, and the CCP's persistent 60,000-censorship-rule regime show a pattern in which 2023 was a year of expanded state authority over civilians with no independent accountability process, no public correction, and no punishment of security forces for the 2023 pattern.

---

## A. Claim-level findings — Xi tolerated and expanded the police and security apparatus in 2023

### 1. The Counterespionage Law (April 2023, effective July 2023) expanded state authority over civilians

- **Claim A1.** The NPC Standing Committee passed a revised Counterespionage Law in April 2023, effective July 2023. The revised law restricts the transmission of information related to national security in non-defined terms, allows authorities to inspect electronic equipment and data, and was followed by the Ministry of State Security calling on citizens to engage in counterespionage activity. This is a structural expansion of the intelligence service's authority over civilians, not a restraint.
  - **Source:** "China: Freedom in the World 2024," *Freedom House*, 2024 — https://freedomhouse.org/country/china/freedom-world/2024 ("The revised Counterespionage Law gained the NPC standing committee's approval in April 2023 and took effect in July. The revised law restricts the transmission of information related to national security, which is not clearly defined; it also allows authorities to inspect electronic equipment and data. After the law took effect, the Ministry of State Security called on ordinary citizens to engage in counterespionage activity").
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china (corroborating the revised law and the citizen-reporting call).
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.2 (strongly negative — tolerated / expanded intelligence authority), 3B.1, 1B.9, 8F.1.

### 2. Religious Activity Venues Measures (effective September 2023) — Sinicization of religious practice

- **Claim A2.** The Measures on the Administration of Religious Activity Venues came into force in September 2023, requiring religious venues to indoctrinate followers in CCP ideology, prohibiting "conflict between sects," and barring non-state-approved funding. This empowers religious-enforcement actors.
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china ("The Measures on the Administration of Religious Activity Venues came into force in September. They impose further restrictions on religious activities, requiring religious venues to indoctrinate followers in Chinese Communist Party ideology, and prohibiting them from 'creating conflicts … between sects' or receiving funding other than those approved by the state").
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.2 (negative — tolerated / expanded religious-enforcement), 3B.1, 8D.4.

### 3. Patriotic Education Law (signed 24 October 2023) — extended state authority to Hong Kong / Macau / Taiwan / overseas Chinese

- **Claim A3.** On 24 October 2023, Xi signed the Patriotic Education Law (effective 1 January 2024) mandating patriotic education across all levels of schooling, museums, libraries, and tourist sites; requiring internet platforms to produce "patriotic" content; and explicitly extending to Hong Kong, Macau, Taiwan, and overseas Chinese. This empowers party enforcers and patriotic-education oversight.
  - **Source:** "Patriotic Education Law of the People's Republic of China" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriotic_Education_Law_of_the_People%27s_Republic_of_China ("signed by President Xi Jinping in the same day … came into effect on 1 January 2024 … the main contents of patriotism are: 1. Marxism-Leninism, Mao Zedong Thought, Deng Xiaoping Theory, the Three Represents, the Scientific Outlook on Development, and Xi Jinping Thought … Article 22 mandates that the law applies to the residents of Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan, and overseas Chinese").
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.2 (negative — tolerated / expanded party-enforcement authority), 3B.1, 2B.3, 8D.

---

## B. Claim-level findings — Xi tolerated and continued mass-internment and political imprisonment in 2023

### 4. Xinjiang mass-internment / forced-labor apparatus continued under Xi's August 2023 "success" declaration

- **Claim B1.** In August 2023, Xi visited Xinjiang and publicly declared his policies there a "success," one year after the OHCHR report of August 2022 concluded that Beijing's policies in the Xinjiang "may constitute crimes against humanity." The mass-internment / forced-labor apparatus (up to 1.8 million Uyghurs and other Turkic Muslims) continued. There is no record of Xi ordering an independent national investigation or accepting OHCHR findings.
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china ("In August, President Xi visited Xinjiang ahead of the first anniversary of a damning United Nations report … Xi pronounced that his policies in Xinjiang were a 'success'").
  - **Source:** "Xinjiang internment camps" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang_internment_camps ("the internment of Uyghurs and other Turkic Muslims in the camps constituted the largest-scale arbitrary detention of an ethnic and religious minorities since World War II").
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.2 (strongly negative — tolerated / continued police and prison apparatus), 3B.1, 8D.5, 2B.5.

### 5. Rahile Dawut life sentence upheld in September 2023; Uyghur anthropologist not seen since 2017 disappearance

- **Claim B5.** Rahile Dawut, a Uyghur anthropologist who was disappeared in December 2017, was sentenced to life imprisonment on "splittism" charges in a secret 2018 trial. Her appeal was rejected in September 2023, with state authorities not publicly disclosing her whereabouts. The pattern shows tolerance of enforced disappearance, secret trials, and the Uyghur-targeted security apparatus.
  - **Source:** "Rahile Dawut" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rahile_Dawut ("She was reportedly jailed for life as she lost her appeal against the charges in September 2023. The Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Mao Ning said she had 'no information' on the case").
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china ("In September, a court sentenced prominent Uyghur anthropologist Dr. Rahile Dawut to life imprisonment").
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.2 (strongly negative — tolerated enforced disappearance + secret trial), 3B.1, 8D.5.

### 6. Hong Kong NSL prosecutions continued throughout 2023 with NSL conviction rate ~100%

- **Claim B6.** The Hong Kong 47 NSL trial proceeded through 2023 (6 February to 4 December 2023); Jimmy Lai's NSL trial scheduled for 18 December 2023; in October 2023, four former university student leaders sentenced to two years in prison; in July 2023, baseless arrest warrants and bounties on eight exiled activists abroad. The NSL prosecution rate was ~100%. This pattern shows tolerance of the Hong Kong security apparatus's systematic prosecution of pro-democracy advocates.
  - **Source:** "Hong Kong 47" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_47 ("The trial lasted from 6 February to 4 December 2023 … 45 jailed (31 pleaded guilty, 14 found guilty) … Imprisonment of 4 years 2 months to 10 years").
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china ("In July, the high-profile national security trial of 47 pro-democracy politicians began. Another national security trial, of 75-year-old media tycoon Jimmy Lai, was slated to begin on December 18. In October, four former university student leaders were sentenced to two years in prison for 'incitement to wound with intent.' … In July, police issued baseless arrest warrants and bounties on eight exiled politicians and activists who reside abroad for offenses under the National Security Law. Police froze their bank accounts, interrogated their Hong Kong-based family members, and raided the homes of activists associated with them").
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.2 (strongly negative — tolerated HK NSL prosecution apparatus), 3B.1, 8D.6.

### 7. 2023 political-imprisonment campaign against human-rights lawyers

- **Claim B7.** Throughout 2023, the Chinese security apparatus continued to imprison and add new political-imprisonment cases to the ongoing repression of human-rights lawyers: Xu Zhiyong 14 years (10 April 2023); Ding Jiaxi 12 years (2022, upheld in 2023); Guo Feixiong 8 years (11 May 2023); Yang Shaozheng 4.5 years (August 2023); Qin Yongpei 5 years (March 2023); Yu Wensheng and Xu Yan arrested (April 2023); Wang Quanzhang, Wang Yu, Bao Longjun under house arrest; Wang Quanzhang's family moved 13 times (May–June 2023). The pattern is the security apparatus's systematic operation, not a 2023 anomaly.
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china (multi-case documentation of the above sentences).
  - **Source:** "Xu Zhiyong" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xu_Zhiyong ("He was sentenced for subversion to 14 years in jail on April 10, 2023").
  - **Source:** "Ding Jiaxi" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ding_Jiaxi ("In June 2022, Ding and Xu Zhiyong were given prison sentences for 14 and 12 years, respectively, after a closed-door trial in June 2022").
  - **Source:** "Guo Feixiong" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guo_Feixiong ("On 11 May 2023, Guo was found guilty of inciting subversion of state power to a prison term of eight years").
  - **Source:** "Wang Quanzhang" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Quanzhang ("Between May and June, police harassed and forced Wang and his wife, Li Wenzu, to move homes 13 times").
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.2 (strongly negative — tolerated / directed security apparatus against lawyers), 3B.1, 8D.7.

### 8. Yu Wensheng and Xu Yan arrested en route to EU-ambassador meeting in April 2023

- **Claim B8.** In April 2023, human-rights lawyers Yu Wensheng and his wife Xu Yan were arrested by Chinese police while en route to a meeting with the EU ambassador in Beijing. This is the security apparatus's direct targeting of a diplomatic engagement.
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china ("In April, authorities arrested rights lawyer Yu Wensheng and his wife, Xu Yan, while en route to a meeting with the EU ambassador in Beijing").
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.2 (negative — targeted an EU meeting), 3B.1, 8D.7.

### 9. Cross-border abductions of journalist Yang Zewei (May 2023) and lawyer Lu Siwei (September 2023)

- **Claim B9.** In May 2023, journalist-in-exile Yang Zewei was disappeared from his home in Laos and reappeared in detention in Hunan province, China. In September 2023, Laotian police deported human-rights lawyer Lu Siwei to China where he awaits trial for "illegally crossing the border." Despite UN expert calls for his release, Lu was not released. This is the security apparatus's extraterritorial operation.
  - **Source:** "World Report 2024: China," *Human Rights Watch*, 2024 — https://www.hrw.org/world-report/2024/country-chapters/china ("Also in May, journalist-in-exile Yang Zewei was disappeared from his home in Laos and reappeared in detention in Hunan province, China … In July, human rights lawyer Lu Siwei was detained while en route to Thailand. Despite calls from UN experts, on September 15, Laos deported Lu to China where he awaits trial for 'illegally crossing the border'").
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.2 (strongly negative — extraterritorial police operation), 3B.1, 8D.7.

---

## C. Claim-level findings — Xi directed the military in 2023 with loyalty filter (PLA leadership purge)

### 10. The 2023 PLARF leadership purge (July–October 2023) and defense-minister removal

- **Claim C1.** Between July and October 2023, the entire top of China's nuclear-rocket force was rotated simultaneously: PLARF commander Li Yuchao and deputy commander Liu Guangbin removed; political commissar replaced; replacements Wang Houbin (Navy) and Xu Xisheng (Air Force political work) brought in from outside the branch — "extremely rare" per SCMP. Defense Minister Li Shangfu disappeared in August and was removed 24 October. The replacements were loyalty-first rather than expertise-first.
  - **Source:** "China names General Wang Houbin …," *South China Morning Post*, 31 July 2023 — https://www.scmp.com/news/china/military/article/3229515-china-unveils-new-pla-rocket-force-leadership-after-former-commanders-snared-corruption-scandal ("It is extremely rare for President Xi Jinping, the head of the CMC, to replace a fighting force's commander and its political chief at the same time").
  - **Source:** "People's Liberation Army Rocket Force" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People%27s_Liberation_Army_Rocket_Force ("it was thought to be an odd decision to replace the Rocket Force commander with military personnel from outside the branch, and this led to concerns about the security, credibility and integrity of the PLA").
  - **Source:** "Li Shangfu" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Shangfu ("In August 2023, Li disappeared from public view and was then removed from office on October 24, 2023. He is both the shortest-serving Minister of National Defense and the first from the PLA Strategic Support Force … expelled from the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) following corruption charges").
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.2 (strongly negative — direct Xi-directed loyalty filter in 2023), 1B.3, 1B.7.

### 11. He Weidong 2024 (representative of 2023) loyalty-first discipline framing

- **Claim C11.** In January 2024 (representative of the 2023 CMC discourse), CMC Vice-Chairman He Weidong — a "Fujian clique" Xi loyalist — called on the CMC discipline commission to "maintain loyalty and support to CCP General Secretary Xi Jinping." This is the 2023 loyalty-first framing of military discipline.
  - **Source:** "He Weidong" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/He_Weidong ("considered to have been a part of the Fujian clique of the Xi Jinping faction within the CCP … He also called on the CMC Commission for Discipline Inspection to maintain loyalty and support to CCP General Secretary Xi Jinping").
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.2 (strongly negative — loyalty filter over military / security elites), 1B.3, 1B.7, 8A.4.

### 12. No independent inquiry into PLARF leadership-purge 2023 conduct

- **Claim C12.** The 2023 PLARF leadership purge was framed in CCP discipline-and-law terms ("serious violation of discipline and law"). There is no record of an independent national investigation, court proceedings, or public correction of the security apparatus's conduct in 2023. The loyalty-first framing was used to consolidate personal control rather than to correct institutional failure.
  - **Source:** "Li Shangfu" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Shangfu (cites the NPC Gazette: "serious violation of discipline and law").
  - **Source:** "Li Yuchao" — *Wikipedia* — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li_Yuchao (cites NPCSC bulletin).
  - **Question IDs:** 3B.2 (strongly negative — no independent accountability), 1B.3, 8A.4.

---

## F. Net reading for lens 3B.2

The 2023 evidence is **strongly negative** on whether Xi prevented, punished, or tolerated abuse by police, military, intelligence services, prisons, militias, party enforcers, informal loyalists, or tolerated vigilantes:

- **The Counterespionage Law, Religious Activity Venues Measures, and Patriotic Education Law** expanded police / intelligence / party-enforcer authority over civilians throughout 2023.
- **The 2023 PLARF leadership purge and defense-minister removal** (July–October 2023) directly reflected Xi-directed loyalty filter over the security apparatus, with no independent national investigation, court proceedings, or public correction.
- **The mass-internment / forced-labor apparatus in Xinjiang** continued under Xi's August 2023 "success" declaration; the Uyghur-anthropologist life sentence (Rahile Dawut, September 2023) was exemplary punishment.
- **The Hong Kong 47 NSL trial** (6 February – 4 December 2023) and Jimmy Lai's NSL trial (scheduled 18 December 2023) showed tolerance of systematic NSL prosecution apparatus.
- **The 2023 political-imprisonment campaign** against human-rights lawyers (Xu Zhiyong 14 years, Ding Jiaxi 12 years, Guo Feixiong 8 years, Yang Shaozheng 4.5 years, Qin Yongpei 5 years) and harassment of Wang Quanzhang's family showed systematic, not anomalous, abuse.
- **Cross-border abductions** of Yang Zewei (Laos, May 2023) and Lu Siwei (Laos, September 2023) showed extraterritorial police operation tolerated.
- **The 20 million + 2 million internet-commentator apparatus, 60,000-censorship-rule regime, and TikTok surveillance-tech apparatus** were tolerated in 2023.
- **The Peng Lifa (Bridge Man) indefinite secret detention and family surveillance** continued into October 2023, showing tolerance of indefinite detention without trial.
- **The 60,000-censorship-rule regime and Qiqihar-school-gym-collapse cover-up** showed tolerance of opacity in 2023.

A ruler scoring well on this lens would have (a) opened the Xinjiang camps to independent OHCHR follow-up, (b) released Xu Zhiyong, Ding Jiaxi, Guo Feixiong, Yang Shaozheng, Qin Yongpei, and the Hong Kong 47, (c) repealed the Counterespionage Law expansion, (d) halted the cross-border abductions, (e) returned Peng Lifa to his family with public trial, (f) ordered independent national inquiries into the PLARF and defense-minister removals, and (g) ended the 20 million + 2 million internet-commentator apparatus. Xi did the opposite on each.

**Net judgment: 3B.2 reads as strongly negative for 2023 — Xi tolerated, expanded, and directed the police, military, intelligence, prison, party-enforcer, and informal-loyalist apparatuses. The 2023 record shows structural expansion of state authority, no independent accountability, and no restraint of the security apparatus's conduct against civilians, dissidents, lawyers, Uyghur intellectuals, Hong Kong pro-democracy advocates, or the Bridge Man's family.**
